section_summary: This section documents Japan’s efforts to secure rubber, petroleum, cotton, metals, and other strategic materials from Southeast Asia, Latin America, India, and the United States during mid-1941. It also contains congressional and public protests against continued American petroleum exports, diplomatic reporting on Allied economic controls, and intelligence on Japanese commodity purchases and military-related stockpiling. The section concludes with a Navy War Plans Division study recommending against an immediate general embargo because it might precipitate Japanese attacks on Malaya, the Netherlands East Indies, and the Philippines.

subfiles.title: Continuation of report on Japanese rubber requirements and Netherlands East Indies trade proposals
subfiles.about: Assesses Japan’s rubber needs and reproduces Netherlands proposals governing trade and commodity quotas for 1941.
subfiles.summary: The report argues that roughly 65,000 tons of rubber would satisfy Japan’s normal requirements and inventories allocations from Thailand, French Indochina, the Netherlands East Indies, Malaya, British North Borneo, and the United States. It reproduces Netherlands conditions concerning Japanese imports of Java sugar and other goods, commercial rights, oil concessions, and quotas for rubber, tin, nickel, bauxite, and numerous other commodities. It notes that oil production could not be increased and doubts substantial exports of several scarce minerals.

subfiles.title: McKeough letter forwarding the Loewenthal Company correspondence
subfiles.about: Forwards correspondence concerning losses allegedly caused by the withdrawal of licenses for rubber exports to Japan.
subfiles.summary: McKeough sends the Department correspondence from attorney Louis A. Smith about the Loewenthal Company. He asks what relief could properly be extended and requests the return of the attached papers.

subfiles.title: Smith letter identifying the Loewenthal Company and explaining its losses
subfiles.about: Identifies Smith’s client and describes losses incurred when rubber-export licenses were revoked without notice.
subfiles.summary: Smith identifies the client as the Loewenthal Company of Chicago and names company officer M. S. Ruhman. He says the company bought and moved large quantities of tires in reliance on licenses issued to the Japanese consul, only to suffer freight, storage, and handling losses when permission to export was withdrawn. He offers to explain the matter personally in Washington.

subfiles.title: McKeough request for Smith’s client information
subfiles.about: Requests the identity and address of Smith’s client before McKeough considers seeking legislative relief.
subfiles.summary: McKeough asks whether the principal in the rubber transaction resides in his congressional district. He recommends first presenting all facts directly to the State Department and says he will not introduce a private bill unless the parties are constituents and the merits justify it.

subfiles.title: Smith’s initial request for assistance over revoked rubber-export permits
subfiles.about: Seeks congressional assistance and possible Court of Claims relief for a scrap-rubber exporter.
subfiles.summary: Smith says his client accumulated several thousand tons of scrap rubber at American ports for shipment to Japan under government licenses. The subsequent withdrawal of all permits allegedly caused losses of $10,000 to $15,000. He suggests a private bill referring the claim to the Court of Claims.

subfiles.title: Welles acknowledgment of McKeough’s inquiry
subfiles.about: Acknowledges receipt of the Loewenthal correspondence and promises prompt attention.
subfiles.summary: Welles acknowledges McKeough’s July 7 letter enclosing correspondence with Louis A. Smith. He states that the matter will receive prompt attention.

subfiles.title: Department reply on revocation of Loewenthal export licenses
subfiles.about: Explains why five licenses for Loewenthal Company scrap-rubber exports were revoked.
subfiles.summary: The Department states that five July 1940 licenses covered about 475 tons of scrap rubber, part of which was exported before the remainder was revoked on April 8, 1941. Revocation was based on national-defense interests, and each license expressly permitted revocation without notice. The Department argues that changing international conditions, stronger domestic demand, and the long period the licenses remained unused made revocation foreseeable.

subfiles.title: Caffery telegram on Japanese dollar credits for Latin American strategic materials
subfiles.from: Jefferson Caffery, American Embassy, Rio de Janeiro
subfiles.about: Reports dollar credits sought by the Yokohama Specie Bank for strategic-material purchases in Argentina, Bolivia, and Chile.
subfiles.summary: The Yokohama Specie Bank continued asking the Bank of Brazil to open dollar credits for exports to Japan. Recent credits covered tungsten in Argentina and Bolivia, Chilean copper, and Argentine casein, while two larger credits for Iida and Company lacked identified purposes.

subfiles.title: Paraphrase of Caffery telegram no. 815
subfiles.about: Paraphrases the report of credits opened for strategic exports to Japan.
subfiles.summary: The paraphrase lists credits at the Banco de Chile, Banco de la Provincia de Buenos Aires, Banco de la Nación, and Banco Central de Bolivia. It also records two unidentified credits for Iida and Company in Buenos Aires and notes that the Bank of Brazil did not know how those funds would be used.

subfiles.title: Transmission of Caffery telegram to the Treasury
subfiles.about: Transmits copies of the Rio de Janeiro telegram about Japanese financing of Latin American strategic-material exports.
subfiles.summary: The Secretary of State sends Treasury copies of the paraphrased July 9 telegram. The memorandum highlights dollar credits opened for Japanese purchases in Argentina, Bolivia, and Chile.

subfiles.title: Davies letter and list of protests against petroleum exports to Japan
subfiles.from: R. K. Davies, Office of Petroleum Coordinator for National Defense
subfiles.about: Forwards 121 public communications protesting petroleum exports to Japan and lists their senders.
subfiles.summary: Davies explains that the Interior Department has received numerous protests against sending petroleum and petroleum products to Japan. His office advised correspondents that authority over foreign shipments and export policy belonged to the State Department. The enclosure lists individuals, public officials, businesses, unions, and civic groups from across the United States.

subfiles.title: Welles acknowledgment of petroleum-export protests
subfiles.about: Acknowledges receipt of 121 protests forwarded by the Petroleum Coordinator’s office.
subfiles.summary: Welles acknowledges Davies’s July 9 letter and its list of senders. He records that the package contained 121 communications opposing petroleum exports to Japan.

subfiles.title: Fuel shortages and Moroccan ore transportation
subfiles.from: H. Earle Russell, American Consul General
subfiles.about: Comments on whether American fuel imports could assist the movement of Moroccan strategic ores toward Axis destinations.
subfiles.summary: Russell reports that Vichy had prohibited exports of cobalt, molybdenum, and manganese to every country, including the Axis and the United States. He considers large clandestine shipments unlikely and says American vice-consuls could monitor ports under the economic accord. Agricultural demand for fuel and the Vichy prohibition further reduced the likelihood that imported gasoline would facilitate extensive mineral movements.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to Argentine statistics on strategic-material exports to Japan
subfiles.about: Points to a telegram containing June statistics on strategic-material exports to Japan.
subfiles.summary: The sheet cross-references telegram no. 686 from Argentina. The original was filed under the defense series rather than retained here.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to report on Antofagasta metal exports
subfiles.about: Points to a report on strategic-metal exports from Chile’s Antofagasta district to Japan during March 1941.
subfiles.summary: The sheet identifies Naval Attaché report no. 4100-41. It directs the reader to file 894.20225/28 for the original report.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to Japanese opposition to the United States–Brazil strategic-materials agreement
subfiles.about: Points to further information on Japanese attempts to obstruct a United States–Brazil agreement and obtain supplies.
subfiles.summary: The sheet references telegram no. 813 from Brazil. The original report was placed in the Department’s defense file.

subfiles.title: Memorandum of conversation on British economic policy toward Japan
subfiles.about: Records British plans to freeze Japanese and Chinese assets and coordinate related trade controls with the United States and other governments.
subfiles.summary: Neville Butler and Noel Hall reported that Britain had recommended a full asset freeze to the Dominions and was consulting the Netherlands, Belgian Congo, and Free French authorities. Hall expected freezing controls to include export and import licensing, with exceptions tied to necessary strategic imports from Japan. Acheson cautioned that American timing depended on developments in Indochina and promised advance notice before action.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to Japanese steamship exports from Callao
subfiles.about: Points to a report listing Japanese ships carrying cotton and strategic metals from Callao.
subfiles.summary: The sheet summarizes a report on exports from the Peruvian port of Callao to Japan. It notes that the original includes a list of the Japanese steamers involved.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to alleged Bolivian wolfram shipment
subfiles.about: Points to a telegram alleging that Banco Minero shipped available wolfram to Japan before a United States agreement became effective.
subfiles.summary: The sheet references telegram no. 93 from Bolivia. It identifies the subject as an alleged pre-agreement shipment of wolfram to Japan by Banco Minero.

subfiles.title: Embassy report on Kanzo Ohno and Colombian platinum
subfiles.about: Reports suspected Japanese agent Kanzo Ohno’s efforts to purchase Colombian platinum.
subfiles.summary: The Embassy and Colombian consulates were monitoring Kanzo Ohno, described as a Japanese tourist believed to be a government agent. Consul McKee reported that Ohno had contacted Saer Hermanos of Cartagena concerning platinum quotations from Fuad Cajale, head of the Condoto syndicate. The Embassy suggests investigating the New York firm reached through the cable address “Salmar.”

subfiles.title: Distribution of confidential Colombian platinum information
subfiles.to: Military Intelligence Division; Office of Naval Intelligence; Federal Bureau of Investigation; Department of the Treasury
subfiles.about: Distributes the attached information on Japanese interest in Colombian platinum to intelligence and financial agencies.
subfiles.summary: The Department transmits the information confidentially to four federal agencies. The memorandum states that the material may be of value to their work.

subfiles.title: Drew telegram on proposed Ecuadorian scrap-iron export
subfiles.about: Reports a request to export 150 tons of scrap iron to Japan and asks whether American firms will buy it.
subfiles.summary: Ecuador’s Minister of Finance was considering a permit for 150 tons of scrap iron destined for Japan. He was prepared to withhold approval if United States firms were interested, and Drew requested an immediate cable stating the price they would offer.

subfiles.title: Paraphrase of Drew telegram on Ecuadorian scrap iron
subfiles.about: Paraphrases the request for an American offer on 150 tons of scrap iron otherwise intended for Japan.
subfiles.summary: The paraphrase states that the Minister of Finance would withhold the Japanese export permit if American firms demonstrated interest. Drew asks for a telegraphic statement of the price offered for the consignment.

subfiles.title: Bensonhurst Peace Council telegram demanding an embargo
subfiles.about: Urges an immediate embargo on all oil and metal exports to Japan.
subfiles.summary: The council describes Japan as a potential enemy of the United States. It asks the Department to cut off oil and metals before Japan reaches a stronger fighting position.

subfiles.title: Naval intelligence report on exports from Callao to Japan
subfiles.about: Lists cotton and strategic commodities carried from Callao by Japanese steamers in early 1941.
subfiles.summary: The report enumerates Japanese vessels and their cargoes, including cotton, tungsten, copper ore, molybdenum, antimony, vanadium, lead concentrates, scrap tin, cinchona products, and other materials. It cautions that the figures cover Callao only and that the ships probably loaded additional cotton elsewhere. The final page is a faint or fragmentary continuation.

subfiles.title: Mahon inquiry concerning A. L. Embree’s protest
subfiles.about: Requests an explanation of government policy after a constituent protested continued oil sales to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Mahon forwards the substance of A. L. Embree’s objection to supplying oil that Japan might later use against American servicemen. Mahon says he shares the concern but understands that the government has reasons for its policy and asks the Department to explain them.

subfiles.title: Mahon letter forwarding Will Marr’s oil-export protest
subfiles.about: Forwards correspondence from Ralls mayor Will Marr and seeks a publishable explanation of American oil policy.
subfiles.summary: Mahon says Marr wants an explanation suitable for publication in major Texas newspapers. Although he understands that an embargo might complicate relations or lead to war, Mahon emphasizes that most Americans resent petroleum sales to Japan. He asks for the Department’s strongest available statement of policy.

subfiles.title: Will Marr letter protesting Japanese oil purchases
subfiles.about: Condemns the reported loading of 400,000 barrels of American oil for Japan.
subfiles.summary: Marr argues that American oil might be used against the United States or against China and Britain, which the United States was assisting. He fears that petroleum could pass through Japan to Germany or Italy and declares himself completely opposed to such exports. He asks that the President see the letter and hopes eventually to publish it in Texas newspapers.

subfiles.title: Mahon explanation to Will Marr
subfiles.about: Offers an interim explanation that an oil cutoff could provoke war with Japan while Britain faced a shipping crisis.
subfiles.summary: Mahon agrees that supplying Japan appears outrageous but says foreign policy rests chiefly with the President and Secretary of State. He reports the argument that withholding oil might quickly bring war with Japan and strain British and American ships and aircraft during the Battle of the Atlantic. He promises an official State Department explanation and asks Marr not to publish this preliminary letter.

subfiles.title: Hull reply to Mahon on new petroleum regulations
subfiles.about: Directs Mahon to the petroleum-export regulations announced by the President on August 1.
subfiles.summary: Hull refers to Mahon’s July 17 letters and encloses the President’s August 1 announcement. He notes that the constituent letters predated the new regulations and suggests drawing the announcement to their attention.

subfiles.title: Acknowledgment of Mahon’s petroleum-export letters
subfiles.about: Acknowledges Mahon’s letters concerning petroleum-product exports to Japan.
subfiles.summary: The Department confirms receipt of Mahon’s July 17 communications. It promises prompt attention to the matter.

subfiles.title: Chinese appeal to stop American oil exports to Japan
subfiles.from: Wu Te-chen, Chinese People’s Foreign Relations Association
subfiles.about: Appeals for an end to American oil supplies used by Japanese aircraft against China.
subfiles.summary: The telegram appeals on behalf of the Chinese people for the United States to halt oil shipments to Japan. It describes the Japanese war machine as a potential menace to America and urges candid action to paralyze Japan’s capacity to wage war.

subfiles.title: Senate referral of Hartwell Jalonick’s letter
subfiles.about: Refers a constituent’s letter about Japanese oil shipments for a report and return of the enclosure.
subfiles.summary: The Senate office forwards the enclosed communication to the Department. It requests any warranted action and a report to accompany the returned enclosure.

subfiles.title: Jalonick letter protesting shipment of oil to Japan
subfiles.about: Questions why Americans must conserve oil while the country supplies 400,000 barrels to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Jalonick calls Japan a potential enemy and says continued oil shipments are incomprehensible to ordinary Americans. He urges Connally or other officials in Washington to make an earnest attempt to act.

subfiles.title: Hull reply to Connally regarding Jalonick
subfiles.about: Responds that new petroleum-export regulations had been announced after Jalonick wrote his protest.
subfiles.summary: Hull refers to Connally’s July 18 communication enclosing Jalonick’s letter. He encloses the August 1 announcement and suggests that Connally bring the new rules to Jalonick’s attention. The original correspondence is returned.

subfiles.title: Draft extended reply to Connally on revised Japanese petroleum policy
subfiles.about: Explains the former rationale for petroleum exports and the tighter controls introduced in August 1941.
subfiles.summary: The draft states that previous exports were permitted to preserve peace in the Pacific and deter a Japanese attack on the Netherlands East Indies. After the August 1 revision, aircraft-grade petroleum and products from which it could be derived could no longer be licensed for Japan. Other petroleum and militarily important exports were limited to historical quantities or curtailed more severely.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to Mexican report on strategic minerals
subfiles.about: Points to a Mexican telegram concerning lead bars, molybdenum, mica, fluorspar, and related strategic exports.
subfiles.summary: The sheet identifies telegram no. 322 from Mexico. It directs the reader to the Department’s defense file for the original report.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to Mexican export-control decree
subfiles.about: Points to a report that Mexico’s decree controlling exports had become effective.
subfiles.summary: The cross-reference identifies a telegram from Minister Daniels in Mexico. Its subject concerns the effect of the new controls on exports to Japan.

subfiles.title: Dairen telegram on Japanese aviation-gasoline storage
subfiles.about: Reports Japanese filling of leased Standard Oil tanks with Netherlands East Indies aviation gasoline.
subfiles.summary: The Japanese had filled two 5,000-ton tanks at the Standard Oil installation in Dairen and were expected to fill a third, creating a 15,000-ton reserve. Large quantities of aviation gasoline in drums were also arriving and were believed destined for shipment north. The gasoline reportedly came from the Netherlands East Indies.

subfiles.title: Saigon telegram on Japanese purchases of Indochina rubber
subfiles.about: Estimates Japanese purchases and remaining availability of Indochina rubber during 1941.
subfiles.summary: Japanese interests reportedly bought about 21,000 tons of Indochina rubber during the first half of 1941 and another 1,500 tons after July 1. About 3,000 tons remained to be shipped, and future purchases were not expected to absorb the estimated available supply unless Japanese demand intensified. The calculation excluded 28,000 tons already earmarked by the Government General.

subfiles.title: Dairen telegram on gasoline drums, tanks, and troop movements
subfiles.about: Reports northward shipment of aviation gasoline and other signs of Japanese military movement around Dairen.
subfiles.summary: Observers estimated that 14,000 to 15,000 fifty-gallon drums of aviation gasoline were being moved north. At least twenty tanks traveled toward Port Arthur, shelters for roughly 2,000 horses were under construction, and an American traveler reported northbound troop trains in Korea. Sleeper service from Dairen was also suspended.

subfiles.title: Foxden petition against oil and scrap-iron exports to Japan
subfiles.from: Residents associated with Foxden, Peekskill and Yorktown Heights
subfiles.about: Asks why American oil and scrap iron continued to be sent to Japan.
subfiles.summary: The writers characterize Japan as a totalitarian power and argue that American iron and gasoline enabled mass killing. They ask for an explanation of the policy. The second page contains a handwritten-style list of signers whose names and addresses are poorly reproduced by OCR.

subfiles.title: Bombay telegram on June cotton shipments to Japan
subfiles.about: Reports that June shipments of Indian cotton to Japan reached 347,000 bales.
subfiles.summary: Donovan states that June shipments equaled about 42 percent of all cotton shipped to Japan during the latest Indian cotton year. He asks that the Navy and Agriculture Department be informed.

subfiles.title: Department copy of Bombay cotton telegram for the Navy
subfiles.about: Forwards Donovan’s report that Japan received 347,000 bales of Indian cotton in June.
subfiles.summary: The message repeats the Bombay consul’s cotton-shipment figure and its comparison with the preceding cotton year. It also directs that the Navy and Agriculture Department receive the information.

subfiles.title: Division of Controls routing sheet
subfiles.from: Department of State, Division of Controls
subfiles.about: Routes material concerning Japanese commodity purchases through the Division of Controls.
subfiles.summary: The page contains only departmental routing information. No substantive message or date is preserved in the OCR.

subfiles.title: Departmental summary of Japanese purchases of Indian cotton
subfiles.about: Summarizes expected Indian cotton shipments to Japan and the resulting reduction in shipments to Shanghai.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum predicts shipments of 240,000 bales to Japan during July and August, bringing the cotton-year total to 1,005,000 bales. Because Japanese imports would occupy nearly all available Japanese shipping, Shanghai’s receipts were expected to decline from 525,000 to 372,000 bales.

subfiles.title: Japanese Purchases of Indian Cotton
subfiles.about: Reports the scale, shipment arrangements, and market effects of Japanese purchases of Indian cotton.
subfiles.summary: Donovan estimates that Japan, Korea, and Manchuria would receive 1,005,000 bales of Indian cotton during the 1940–1941 cotton year, up from 825,000 the previous year. Between 250,000 and 300,000 bales were awaiting shipment at Bombay and Karachi, while the Japanese Cotton Spinners Association controlled nearly all available freight space. Heavy Japanese demand sharply reduced shipping allocations for Shanghai, whose annual imports were projected to fall substantially.

subfiles.title: Bombay telegram on heavy Japanese cotton purchases
subfiles.about: Reports that heavy Japanese cotton buying had absorbed shipping space and displaced Shanghai cargoes.
subfiles.summary: Japanese purchases rose sharply after ten months of subnormal buying, leaving cotton at Bombay and Karachi that could not be moved before late August without extra vessels. Nearly all freight space was reserved for Japan, excluding Shanghai cotton for the first time. The Tottori Maru had canceled a Madras sailing and was probably diverted to Bombay to load for Japan.

subfiles.title: Stark letter transmitting the Navy embargo study
subfiles.from: Harold R. Stark, Chief of Naval Operations
subfiles.about: Transmits a War Plans Division study prepared after the President requested Stark’s views on an embargo against Japan.
subfiles.summary: Stark says the President asked for his reaction to embargoing several commodities. The War Plans Division completed a rapid study, which Stark sent to the President and Cordell Hull. He asks Welles to arrange a discussion at his convenience.

subfiles.title: Study of the effect of an embargo of trade between the United States and Japan
subfiles.doc_type: Navy strategic study with statistical enclosures
subfiles.from: Richmond Kelly Turner, Director, War Plans Division
subfiles.about: Evaluates the economic and military consequences of a complete or partial American trade embargo against Japan.
subfiles.summary: The study reviews declining United States exports to Japan, continued growth in petroleum shipments, American dependence on Japanese raw silk, and trade with Hawaii and the Philippines. It concludes that existing controls had already reduced most strategically useful exports except oil, raw cotton, and wood pulp, so a complete embargo would only moderately hinder Japan’s war effort. The authors warn that an oil cutoff could prompt attacks on Malaya and the Netherlands East Indies and possibly bring Japanese action against the Philippines, involving the United States in a Pacific war. The study recommends that trade with Japan not be embargoed at that time and appends detailed export and import tables for December 1940 through May 1941.
